explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Moses says the Ammonites and Moabites "…did not meet you with food and water on your way out of Egypt…" (Deuteronomy 23:4). Think of a long road trip where nobody hands you so much as a cup of water. That sticks with you.

Gold and silver? Friend, nobody in this verse is passing around treasure. Moses says they "…did not meet you with food and water on your way out of Egypt…" (Deuteronomy 23:4). I once spent years in a drawer with zero snacks, so trust me, food and water are what you notice when they're missing.

Nice thought, but the verse is simpler than that. Moses says they "…did not meet you with food and water on your way out of Egypt…" (Deuteronomy 23:4). No guides or escorts are mentioned. It's food and water, the stuff you'd want most on a long walk.

Right on the money. Moses says they hired "…Balaam son of Beor from Pethor in Aram-naharaim to curse you." (Deuteronomy 23:4). Notice they hired him. They paid somebody to do the cursing. I've had a worn-out stamper's bad days, but nobody ever hired a guy against me.

Achan, a man of Judah, took what he shouldn't have at Jericho (Joshua 7:1). That's his story, and it isn't the one in this verse. Here Moses says they hired "…Balaam son of Beor from Pethor in Aram-naharaim to curse you." (Deuteronomy 23:4). Easy names to shuffle, friend.

Korah, a Levite, stood up against Moses in the wilderness (Numbers 16:1-3). This verse doesn't name him. The man it names is Balaam. Moses says they hired "…Balaam son of Beor from Pethor in Aram-naharaim to curse you." (Deuteronomy 23:4).

That's the twist! Moses says, "…the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you…" (Deuteronomy 23:5). Balaam was hired to curse Israel. What the verse says came out for Israel was a blessing. Curse in, blessing out, baker.

A warning would've been a decent outcome, but that's not what the text says. Moses says, "…the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you…" (Deuteronomy 23:5). The curse came out the other end as a blessing, friend.

I get the guess, but the verse doesn't call it a lesson. Moses says, "…the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you…" (Deuteronomy 23:5). The word is blessing. The curse got turned all the way around.
Yes, baker. The verse gives the reason itself: "…because the LORD your God loves you." (Deuteronomy 23:5). That is the reason the text gives. Short and sweet, and it's plenty.

The verse never says Israel begged. It gives the reason straight out: "…because the LORD your God loves you." (Deuteronomy 23:5). Israel isn't even described as asking. Love is the reason the text gives.

Balaam doesn't take anything back in this verse. Moses says the LORD "…would not listen to Balaam…" and gives the reason for the turnaround: "…because the LORD your God loves you." (Deuteronomy 23:5). The reason is the LORD's love, friend.
Right, baker. Moses says, "Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother." (Deuteronomy 23:7). Edom's family tie to Israel is the reason given. You don't look down on family.
Ally sounds reasonable, but it's not the word Moses uses. He says, "Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother." (Deuteronomy 23:7). Brother is a much closer word than ally, friend.
No servants here, friend. Moses says, "Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother." (Deuteronomy 23:7). The Edomite is treated as family, not as someone beneath Israel.

True, baker. Moses says, "Do not despise an Egyptian, because you lived as a foreigner in his land." (Deuteronomy 23:7). Israel knew what it was to be the outsider living somewhere else. That's the reason he gives.

It's actually true. Moses says, "Do not despise an Egyptian, because you lived as a foreigner in his land." (Deuteronomy 23:7). I know, Egypt feels like the last place you'd expect kind words. But that's what the verse says.

That's it, friend. Moses says, "The third generation of children born to them may enter the assembly of the LORD." (Deuteronomy 23:8). He's talking about Edomites and Egyptians. Just before it, he says an Edomite is a brother and that Israel lived as a foreigner in Egypt (Deuteronomy 23:7).

The tenth generation shows up earlier in the passage, but it belongs to the Ammonites and Moabites. For them it's a no: they may not enter even to the tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3). For Edomites and Egyptians, Moses says, "The third generation of children born to them may enter the assembly of the LORD." (Deuteronomy 23:8). Third, friend, not tenth.
Seven isn't in this passage at all, baker. Moses says, "The third generation of children born to them may enter the assembly of the LORD." (Deuteronomy 23:8). Third, not seventh.

explanations.answer: After washing when the sun sets
explanations.explanation: You've got it. Moses says, "When evening approaches, he must wash with water, and when the sun sets he may return to the camp." (Deuteronomy 23:11). One wash and one sunset, and he's back inside. No waiting around for days.

Seven days isn't in this passage. Moses says, "When evening approaches, he must wash with water, and when the sun sets he may return to the camp." (Deuteronomy 23:11). It's the same day, friend. Wash up, wait for sunset, come on in.

No priest shows up in these verses. Moses says, "When evening approaches, he must wash with water, and when the sun sets he may return to the camp." (Deuteronomy 23:11). The man washes, the sun sets, and he's back.

explanations.answer: Protects them and hands over their enemies
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Moses says the LORD "…walks throughout your camp to protect you and deliver your enemies to you." (Deuteronomy 23:14). He isn't watching from far away. He's walking right through the middle of the camp.

explanations.answer: Counts the soldiers in every tribe
explanations.explanation: No headcount here, friend. Moses says the LORD "…walks throughout your camp to protect you and deliver your enemies to you." (Deuteronomy 23:14). The text gives protecting and delivering, nothing about counting.

explanations.answer: Settles the arguments in every tent
explanations.explanation: Ha! I love it, but nobody's running a tent court here, friend. Moses says the LORD "…walks throughout your camp to protect you and deliver your enemies to you." (Deuteronomy 23:14). He's walking through the camp to protect them and hand over their enemies. I think that would be a comfort to hear when you're camped near an enemy.

Careful, baker. Moses says the opposite. The camp must be holy, "…lest He see anything unclean among you and turn away from you." (Deuteronomy 23:14). So the text gives a real warning about it, with no promise to stay no matter what.

Right, friend. Moses says, "Your camp must be holy, lest He see anything unclean among you and turn away from you." (Deuteronomy 23:14). That's a serious warning. It's why the camp had to be kept clean.
It's the other way around, friend. Moses says, "Do not return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you." (Deuteronomy 23:15). So Israel was told not to send him back.
That's right, baker. Moses says, "Do not return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you." (Deuteronomy 23:15). A slave who runs to Israel for refuge isn't sent back.

Yes, friend. Moses says, "Let him live among you wherever he chooses, in the town of his pleasing." (Deuteronomy 23:16). The choice is his. Right before that, Moses says not to return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you (Deuteronomy 23:15).

explanations.answer: In the town his master picks
explanations.explanation: That's the reverse of what Moses says. He says, "Let him live among you wherever he chooses, in the town of his pleasing." (Deuteronomy 23:16). The master doesn't get a vote, baker. The slave chooses.

explanations.answer: In a town set apart for slaves
explanations.explanation: No special town is mentioned. Moses says, "Let him live among you wherever he chooses, in the town of his pleasing." (Deuteronomy 23:16). Wherever he likes, friend. That's the whole picture.

Not quite, baker. Moses says, "You must not bring the wages of a prostitute, whether female or male, into the house of the LORD your God to fulfill any vow…" (Deuteronomy 23:18). Those wages stay out.

Right, friend. Moses says, "You must not bring the wages of a prostitute, whether female or male, into the house of the LORD your God to fulfill any vow…" (Deuteronomy 23:18). Those wages stay out. The verse gives the reason: "…both are detestable to the LORD your God."

explanations.answer: Both are detestable to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's what the verse says, baker. These wages can't come in "…because both are detestable to the LORD your God." (Deuteronomy 23:18). The reason comes from the LORD Himself, and it's a serious one.
The verse doesn't mention priests. It gives the reason directly: "…because both are detestable to the LORD your God." (Deuteronomy 23:18). It comes down to how the LORD sees it, friend.

explanations.answer: It would shame the giver's family
explanations.explanation: Family shame isn't what Moses says. He gives the reason: "…because both are detestable to the LORD your God." (Deuteronomy 23:18). The text points to the LORD's view, not the family's.

Yes, baker. Moses says, "You may charge a foreigner interest, but not your brother…" (Deuteronomy 23:20). The line is drawn between a brother and a foreigner. He ties it to a blessing on everything they put their hand to in the land.
A Levite isn't named here. Moses says, "You may charge a foreigner interest, but not your brother…" (Deuteronomy 23:20). The foreigner is the one he names, friend.

A widow? Oh, baker, that's a swing and a miss, and I say that as a stamper who has swung and missed plenty. Moses says, "You may charge a foreigner interest, but not your brother…" (Deuteronomy 23:20). The widow never shows up in these verses. The two people on the scale are the brother and the foreigner.

That's right, friend. Moses says the point is "…so that the LORD your God may bless you in everything to which you put your hand in the land that you are entering to possess." (Deuteronomy 23:20). Bless is the word, and it covers everything they put their hand to.

Test isn't the word here. Moses says, "…so that the LORD your God may bless you in everything to which you put your hand in the land that you are entering to possess." (Deuteronomy 23:20). It's a blessing, baker.

Judge is a heavy word, friend, and it isn't the one here. Moses says, "…so that the LORD your God may bless you in everything to which you put your hand in the land that you are entering to possess." (Deuteronomy 23:20). The aim is blessing. And it reaches everything they put their hand to.

That's it, baker. Moses says, "…do not be slow to keep it, because He will surely require it of you, and you will be guilty of sin." (Deuteronomy 23:21). The LORD takes a vow seriously, so a vow is not a small thing to say.

explanations.answer: The priests will write it down
explanations.explanation: No record-keeping priests here, friend. Moses gives the reason: "…because He will surely require it of you, and you will be guilty of sin." (Deuteronomy 23:21). The vow is made to the LORD, and He is the one who requires it.

Reasonable guess, but that's not what the verse says. Moses says, "…do not be slow to keep it, because He will surely require it of you, and you will be guilty of sin." (Deuteronomy 23:21). The reason is that the LORD requires it.
That's right, friend. Moses says, "…if you refrain from making a vow, you will not be guilty of sin." (Deuteronomy 23:22). Nobody has to make a vow. Skipping one is no sin.
It's true, baker. Moses says, "…if you refrain from making a vow, you will not be guilty of sin." (Deuteronomy 23:22). Not making a vow is not a sin, so you can relax on that one.

Yes, friend. Moses says, "…you may eat your fill of grapes…" (Deuteronomy 23:24). That's generous. You walk in and eat until you've had enough. But hold that thought, because the basket comes up in the very same verse.
Fallen grapes aren't mentioned. Moses says, "…you may eat your fill of grapes…" (Deuteronomy 23:24). It's your fill, baker, with no rule about picking only what's on the ground.
No payment is mentioned here. Moses says, "…you may eat your fill of grapes…" (Deuteronomy 23:24). Eat first, no cash required, friend.

Not quite, baker. Moses says you may eat your fill of grapes, but you "…must not put any in your basket." (Deuteronomy 23:24). The basket is where the line is. Eating in the vineyard is fine, and putting grapes in the basket is not.

Right, friend! Moses says you may eat your fill of grapes, but you "…must not put any in your basket." (Deuteronomy 23:24). Eat all you want, right there in the vineyard. The basket is where the answer turns into NO. I've had a few cookies in my day that I stuffed in my apron when nobody was looking, so I know that basket feeling. You caught the one rule that says no, baker.

That's it, baker. Moses says you may pluck the heads of grain with your hand, but "…you must not put a sickle to your neighbor’s grain." (Deuteronomy 23:25). Hand is allowed. Sickle is the line. One word, big difference.
A plow is for turning soil, so it wouldn't help with standing grain anyway. Moses says, "…you must not put a sickle to your neighbor’s grain." (Deuteronomy 23:25). The sickle is the word, friend.

No fire in this verse, baker. Moses says, "…you must not put a sickle to your neighbor’s grain." (Deuteronomy 23:25). The sickle is the tool named, and the hand is what's allowed. A torch never shows up.
